claims.claim: Sini says the presence Wolfe's sentences summon has contours that are not clearly defined and yet are not vague.
claims.source: Matthew Sini, 'Great Uncle Gene', New Mythologies (Substack), 2023
claims.quote: its contours aren’t always clearly defined, but it’s also not vague

claims.claim: Sini says much of Wolfe's world is withheld from the reader by the narrowness of the narrator's perception.
claims.source: Matthew Sini, 'Great Uncle Gene', New Mythologies (Substack), 2023
claims.quote: kept from us due to the narrowness of the narrator’s perception

claims.claim: The WolfeWiki novice guide reports Wolfe said he does not give important information twice.
claims.source: WolfeWiki, 'Where to Begin? A Novice's Guide to the Lupine Maze', last modified 2017
claims.quote: he doesn't give the important information twice

claims.claim: The guide advises reading an apparent contradiction as a hint that the narrator is concealing something.
claims.source: WolfeWiki, 'Where to Begin? A Novice's Guide to the Lupine Maze', last modified 2017
claims.quote: Apparent contradictions are often useful hints that the narrator is concealing something.

claims.claim: The guide asserts the information a reader needs is always present in a Wolfe text, though not where the reader expects it.
claims.source: WolfeWiki, 'Where to Begin? A Novice's Guide to the Lupine Maze', last modified 2017
claims.quote: The information you need is always there

claims.claim: The guide says Wolfe works out what a narrator would say rather than what the author wants to say.
claims.source: WolfeWiki, 'Where to Begin? A Novice's Guide to the Lupine Maze', last modified 2017
claims.quote: what they would say, rather than what he wants to say

claims.claim: The guide tells a new reader to begin by asking who is telling the story, when, why, and to whom.
claims.source: WolfeWiki, 'Where to Begin? A Novice's Guide to the Lupine Maze', last modified 2017
claims.quote: Who is telling this story, and when? Why are they telling it

claims.quote: a slight clue to the story in the sentence’s grammar

claims.claim: Keeley reads the absent comma in the phrase naming the narrator's brother as a detail the book later explains.
claims.quote: We eventually do learn why that comma is missing.

claims.claim: Keeley says one first-person sentence near the end of an otherwise third-person Wolfe book makes the reader reconsider all of it.
claims.quote: asks readers to reconsider everything that they’ve already read

claims.claim: Keeley says every word in The Book of the New Sun can be found in a dictionary, so the strangeness is not neologism.

claims.claim: Keeley says the rare words in The Book of the New Sun were chosen to be evocative rather than specific.
claims.quote: chosen to be evocative, rather than specific

claims.claim: Wolfe's appendix to The Shadow of the Torturer, quoted by Keeley, says substituted words like peltast and exultant are meant to be suggestive rather than definitive.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, appendix to The Shadow of the Torturer, quoted by Matthew Keeley (Tor.com, 2017)
claims.quote: are intended to be suggestive rather than definitive

claims.claim: Keeley advises the reader to attend to Severian's sins of omission.
claims.quote: Pay attention to his sins of omission

claims.claim: Keeley says Severian self-justifies and misinterprets but rarely lies outright.
claims.quote: He self-justifies and misinterprets, but rarely lies outright.

verdicts.trueWording: its contours aren't always clearly defined, but it's also not vague
verdicts.note: Live raw page (curl, 200). Quote exact, in the paragraph on Wolfe's sentences as 'mystagogic initiation': 'The presence of "something" is brought forth, and its contours aren't always clearly defined, but it's also not vague.' Page hedges with 'always'; the claim drops it, which is the only drift.

verdicts.trueWording: many aspects of it are also kept from us
verdicts.note: Live raw page. Full sentence: 'The world of New Sun, Urth, is made visible, but many aspects of it are also kept from us due to the narrowness of the narrator's perception, but the narrator's perception of things is all we have to cling to.' Sits in the penultimate body paragraph, matching the cited 'closing section'.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe has said that he doesn't give the important information twice
verdicts.note: Live raw page (curl, 200). Under 'Hints for Beginners': 'Wolfe has said that he doesn't give the important information twice, because he feels his intelligence insulted when other writers do so.' Attribution to Wolfe via the guide is exactly as claimed. Page footer confirms last modified November 17, 2017.

verdicts.trueWording: Apparent contradictions are often useful hints that the narrator is concealing something.
verdicts.note: Live raw page. Sentence stands verbatim as a full sentence opening its paragraph in 'Hints for Beginners', followed by the advice to ask which of X or Y the narrator would prefer to be true.

verdicts.trueWording: The information you need is always there -- but it might not be where you expect it to be
verdicts.note: Live raw page. Quote exact. Both limbs present; note the page hedges the second limb with 'might not be where you expect it to be', where the claim states it flatly. The guide adds: 'If the information you need isn't there, you're probably attacking the wrong question.'

verdicts.trueWording: figures out what they would say, rather than what he wants to say
verdicts.note: Live raw page. Full sentence: 'He goes more deeply into the heads of his narrators, as narrators, than most writers, and figures out what they would say, rather than what he wants to say.' Both limbs (narrator's speech vs author's) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Who is telling this story, and when? Why are they telling it, and to whom?
verdicts.note: Live raw page. Framed as 'some good questions to begin with' on encountering a Lupine text; all four interrogatives (who, when, why, to whom) present, and the guide adds that obvious answers are probably wrong.

verdicts.trueWording: There's also, perhaps, a slight clue to the story in the sentence's grammar
verdicts.note: Live raw page (curl, 200; published November 9, 2017). The sentence under discussion is expressly the opening line of The Fifth Head of Cerberus. Page hedges with 'perhaps, a slight'; the following sentence ('We eventually do learn why that comma is missing') affirms the clue is real.

verdicts.trueWording: We eventually do learn why that comma is missing.
verdicts.note: Live raw page. Preceding sentence supplies the comma limb: 'If the narrator had only one brother, we would read "my brother, David" rather than the comma-less "my brother David."' So the absent comma in the phrase naming the brother, and the later explanation, are both on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: a single sentence in the first person near the very end of a book otherwise in the third person
verdicts.note: Live raw page. Full sentence ends '...asks readers to reconsider everything that they've already read.' Every limb (single first-person sentence, near the very end, otherwise third-person, reconsider all of it) is present; the article's subject throughout is Wolfe.

verdicts.trueWording: It's not that Wolfe strews neologisms over the page - every word in the book appears in a dictionary
verdicts.note: Live raw page (curl, 200; published December 4, 2017), advice 1 'Set aside the dictionary'. Both limbs explicit: the dictionary limb verbatim, the not-neologism limb in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: most of the potentially-unfamiliar words are extremely rare, and chosen to be evocative, rather than specific
verdicts.note: Live raw page, advice 1. The 'rare words' limb is in the same clause, so both limbs of the claim are supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Such words as peltast, androgyn, and exultant are substitutions of this kind, and are intended to be suggestive rather than definitive.
verdicts.note: Live raw page, advice 1, block quotation, introduced as 'In the brief appendix to the first volume, The Shadow of the Torturer, Wolfe introduces himself as the translator...'. Both named words (peltast, exultant) appear; the appendix attribution is Keeley's own framing, as the claim says.

verdicts.trueWording: Pay attention to his sins of omission: the white space between chapters...
verdicts.note: Live raw page, third piece of advice ('Mind the gaps'), matching the cited 'advice 3'. Continues: '...and the gap between one book's end and another's beginning are rarely insignificant.'

verdicts.trueWording: He self-justifies and misinterprets, but rarely lies outright.
verdicts.note: Live raw page, advice 3, immediately after 'Severian is an unreliable narrator for several reasons, but not much of a liar.' Quote is an exact standalone sentence and every limb is supported.
